Thymomas are tumours of the mediastinum, arising from thymic tis- sue. They are rare, and most commonly present in patients between 40 and 60 years of age. Thymoma originates from the epithelium of the thymus but may also contain a lym- phocyte component, which is probably not neoplastic. Up to 50% of patients are asymptomatic, and others have local symptoms such as cough, chest pain, dyspnoea, and ob- struction of the vena cava; paraneoplastic syndromes such as myasthenia gravis, red cell aplasia, and hypogamma- globulinaemia may also develop. Thymomas may be classified based on cell type; they are also staged as non-invasive (encapsulated, stage I), inva- sive (localised, stage II; extensive, stage III; and dissemi- nated, IVa), and metastatic (IVb). The majority of patients present with non-invasive disease, and can be treated sole- ly by surgical resection with low recurrence rates and long- term survival approaching 100%.1-3 Use of adjuvant radi- ation therapy for stage II and III thymoma is controver- sial.4 Some recommend postoperative radiotherapy after complete surgical resection,1,2 whereas others consider it to be beneficial only in patients with incomplete resection; late complications of radiation therapy may occur.4 In patients with unresectable invasive disease, primary ra- diation therapy has been used to shrink the thymoma to make it resectable.2 Radiotherapy alone has also been used, with conflicting results.2 There is increasing interest in combined modality approaches to improve survival in this group.1-4 Chemotherapy has also been used to shrink tumours, allowing for resection.2 Postoperative radiother- apy and/or chemotherapy is then given.2,4,5 Chemotherapy regimens used in this approach are similar to those used in metastatic disease.
